title: 2.4.22 Fix the Infinite Loop
description: A countdown plan arrives whose loop never says when it stops. Find the missing way out and add it, so the plan can finally reach its end.
sourceRef: designed: practice diagnosing an infinite loop on a chart for book 2.4.5, mirrors the 2.2.14 'Fix the Broken Chart' pattern

steps.title: Repair the infinite loop
steps.instructions:
Someone planned a countdown: `count` starts at `5`, prints while it is above `0`, and goes down by `1` each round. Their plan is already in `README.md`, and it is **broken**: its loop says `REPEAT FOREVER`.

The finished plan is drawn as a flow chart above the editor (open the Flow Chart bar). You do not draw it, you **read** it: the diamond asks `is count over 0?`, the `yes` exit goes round the loop, and the `no` exit is the way out.

**Press Grade before you change anything.** Some Quest cards are green and some are red. Read the red ones:

| Red card | What it is complaining about |
|---|---|
| The loop asks count > 0 | The loop never asks a question, so nothing can ever make it stop |
| The loop is closed | The plan never says where the repeating steps end and the plan carries on |

Two red cards, one missing idea: **there is no way out.** Look at the green cards too: `count` starts at 5, it prints, and it goes down. Those are fine, but a loop that counts down and never *tests* the count still runs forever. **An infinite loop is not a plan with no end line. It is a plan whose way out can never be reached.**

Repair the plan; do not start over:

1. Change `REPEAT FOREVER` into a loop with a test: `WHILE count > 0`.
2. Keep the print and the countdown step inside it, indented.
3. After them, close the loop with `END WHILE`, so the plan can carry on to its end.

Keywords, in a different program: `SET lives TO 3`, `WHILE lives > 0` ... `END WHILE`, `PRINT lives`. Plain English is fine. Changing your text clears the marks, so press **Grade** again when you have finished.

Before you submit, trace it by hand: `count` is 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 and prints each time, then count is 0, the test fails, and the loop is over.
hints: A loop needs a question it asks before every round. Which question makes the countdown stop?
WHILE count > 0 ... END WHILE: the steps in between repeat, then the plan carries on after END WHILE.

requirements.title: Numbered steps
requirements.description: Number your steps 1. 2. 3. and so on, with something written after each number.
requirements.hint: Write at least four lines that start with a number, each with a step written after it.

requirements.title: count starts at 5
requirements.description: Set count to 5 before the loop.
requirements.hint: Start with a step that sets count to 5.

requirements.title: The loop prints count
requirements.description: Each round prints the current count.
requirements.hint: Add a step that prints count.

requirements.title: count goes down by 1
requirements.description: Each round count is reduced by 1.
requirements.hint: Add a step that takes 1 off count each round.

requirements.title: The loop asks count > 0
requirements.description: The loop has a test that stops it: it repeats while count is above 0 (or until count reaches 0).
requirements.hint: Give the loop a test: WHILE count > 0.

requirements.title: The loop is closed
requirements.description: The plan shows where the repeating steps end, so it can carry on to its end (END WHILE, "loop ends", "stop").
requirements.hint: Close the loop with END WHILE.

aiCheck.rubricTitle: What the AI read in your steps
aiCheck.prompt: The student was given plain-English steps and rewrote them as numbered, step-by-step pseudocode in README.md, between a first line and a last line that were already there. The program is: let count = 5; while (count > 0) { console.log(count); count = count - 1; } and then the program ends. The plan the student started from said REPEAT FOREVER, with no test and no stopping point, so it is an infinite loop. The point is that a loop needs a test on count that can become false (count > 0) and a place where the loop ends. Judge each criterion ONLY by whether its idea is present in the student's steps, however they word it. Plain English, keywords such as SET, IF, ELSE, END IF, FOR EACH, END FOR, CALL, PRINT, or a mix of both are all fine, and so are different names, different capitalisation, and different ways to number the lines. Do not require any particular keyword. A step that is clearly aimed at the criterion is enough for 'met'. Mark a criterion 'missing' only when the idea is absent or the steps do the opposite (for example a loop that repeats forever or has no test on count, or no line closing the loop). Write each note for THIS student's own steps: in a not-met note, name the exact step or word in their steps that causes the problem (quote at most a few words), say in plain words what it does now versus what the criterion needs, and give one concrete next thing to try, but do NOT write the corrected steps. In a met note, say in one short phrase what in their steps satisfied it. Do not use generic praise.

rubric.title: Numbered steps
rubric.description: The student numbered their steps (1. 2. 3. or similar), at least four of them.

rubric.title: count starts at 5
rubric.description: Set count to 5 before the loop.

rubric.title: The loop prints count
rubric.description: Each round prints the current count.

rubric.title: count goes down by 1
rubric.description: Each round count is reduced by 1.

rubric.title: The loop asks count > 0
rubric.description: The loop is controlled by a real test on count that can stop it, such as WHILE count > 0 or REPEAT UNTIL count is 0. The test must compare count with 0: a test against any other number (for example count > 5 or count < 10) does not meet this. A loop that repeats forever, or with no test on count, does not meet this.

rubric.title: The loop is closed
rubric.description: There is an explicit written line that closes the loop or says it stops (END WHILE, END LOOP, a line saying the loop is over, or a stop when count reaches 0). Indentation alone, with no closing line, does not meet this.
